A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison, despite some internal reporting inconsistencies.

before.justification: V1 reports original NIH evaluations, attention analyses, attention-steering experiments, and conditional fine-tuning results on contextual QA and MT-Bench, including appendix ablations.

after.justification: V2 retains original conditional fine-tuning results and reports expanded NIH and attention analyses, revised steering experiments, and prompt-variation statistics.

M1.justification: Both versions retain the attention-rescaling rule, context-dependency score, threshold-based selection, and indicator-conditioned fine-tuning procedure. V2 supplies head-selection details and reframes attention steering as diagnostic evidence; it does not establish a new method component.

E1.justification: Both use ShareGPT, UltraChat-200K, and WizardLM-70K for fine-tuning and NIH, SQuAD, QuAC, DROP, and MT-Bench for evaluation. The extensions concern model configurations, context-window settings, and prompt sensitivity within retained task coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Table 1 adds inference without a chat template as an explicit reference within the attention-steering comparison; v1 Table 2 compared steering factors against unsteered inference. The main conditional fine-tuning comparison retains vanilla fine-tuning and the official Llama-2/Llama-3 reference models.

E3.justification: NIH evaluation expands from four to eight base/instruct model pairs and introduces four-template testing for smaller configurations. V1's steering grid across three models and three fine-tuning datasets is replaced by two official Llama-2 chat models, selecting alpha from six candidates. MT-Bench now includes the indicator by default instead of omitting it, and the main results table adds a cross-task average.

E4.justification: V2 expands attention-allocation diagnostics from two to seven models, adds prompt-sensitivity testing and a threshold-versus-selected-fraction analysis, and replaces the broad steering-factor ablation with a focused intervention study. The original threshold-performance ablation, layer-disagreement heatmap, and instruction-length distributions remain in the appendices.

E5.justification: V2 Appendix A.2 and Tables 7–8 introduce means and standard deviations across four NIH prompt templates for smaller configurations; v1 reports single estimates. These statistics measure prompt variation, not variation across training seeds. Larger evaluations still use one template.

E6.justification: V2 adds NIH results for Llama-2-13B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-2-9B/27B, replaces some existing estimates with prompt averages, and reports new steering and selection-fraction results. All contextual-task entries in v1 Table 3 are retained in v2 Table 4, but most indicator-model MT-Bench scores change under the revised indicator setting: for example, UltraChat/Llama-3 changes from 7.2750 to 6.8500. This is not a same-setting performance decline.

T1.justification: The attention-rescaling and context-dependency-score equations are unchanged. Appendix B.3 expresses the previously described highest-user-attention head choice as an argmax; this formalizes existing selection logic rather than adding a theoretical result or proof.

C1.justification: V2 removes attention steering from the headline list of proposed mitigation techniques and promotes the existing context-dependency metric as a separate contribution. It explicitly anchors the identification claim to NIH performance with chat templates, while retaining the central bias explanation and conditional fine-tuning claim.

C2.justification: V2 elaborates the mechanism through attention balancing between user-context and assistant-response consistency. It interprets dataset sparsity as support for learned role bias and connects MT-Bench behavior to subset diversity. It also adds explicit computational and QLoRA limitations while retaining the indicator-confounding and user-selection limitations.

D1.justification: V2 documents head selection per input or sampled NIH prompt and lists four exact NIH prompt templates. It drops v1's explicit first-round QuAC restriction and 80-response MT-Bench count without establishing changed sampling. Training recipes, epoch counts, and code-access information remain. The stated 4K–32K context range conflicts with Table 7's 128K entry.

R1.justification: Related work is substantially recast around intrinsic hallucination, positional versus role bias, catastrophic forgetting, and RLHF side effects. V2 adds works including Huang et al., Liu et al. on Lost in the Middle, Kirkpatrick et al., and Wu et al., while removing the conditional-SFT discussion of SteerLM, Korbak et al., and Chain of Hindsight.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, methodological explanations, results narrative, and conclusion are extensively rewritten. Related work moves from Section 2 to Section 5, and attention steering moves into the diagnostic section before the standalone conditional fine-tuning method. This substantially changes the narrative structure.

P2.justification: The NIH chart is expanded and the attention chart is redesigned, with an additional absolute-attention figure. The steering table is replaced, dataset statistics are split from selection ratios, and prompt and average-score displays are added. Existing appendix plots are retained and relocated. Table 4 also incorrectly bolds the 6.8500 MT-Bench score below its 7.2375 baseline.

improvement.justification: V2 strengthens support for the central chat-template effect through broader model diagnostics and four-template variability reporting, and makes head selection more reproducible. Testing MT-Bench with the indicator present also exposes the practical tradeoff more directly. These gains are limited by the narrower steering study, inconsistent NIH reference values between Tables 1 and 7, and erroneous highlighting in Table 4; the main contextual fine-tuning results remain unchanged.
